purpose: Every question that must be answered before a decision can be reasonably made, split into what the repository already contains and what it does not, with the specific official page or action that would close each gap. Where no official source can answer a question, that is stated as the answer rather than guessed around.

codes.state: ANSWERED = resolved from an official source inside this session, with the source link. OPEN = not answerable from the current evidence. IMPOSSIBLE = cannot be answered from official sources at all; the reason is given.
codes.blocks: The decision that cannot be taken until the question is closed.

questions.question: What is the latest official result set, and does the repository's own game log agree with it?
questions.have: A 137-game official log: the inherited, previously verified Weeks 1-8 rows (121 games), 15 Week 9 games transcribed fresh from nfl.com/scores/2026/week-9, and the completed Week 10 Thursday game (WAS 24 NYG 21) transcribed from nfl.com/scores/2026/week-10.
questions.answer: Recomputing W-L-T, PCT, PF, PA, NET, HOME and ROAD from that log reproduces the official standings exactly: 352 of 352 cells match across all 32 clubs.
questions.resolution: https://www.nfl.com/standings/league/2026/REG compared against requirements/data/raw-standings-2026-11-14.txt by requirements/scripts/verify_capture.py

questions.question: Did the Week 9 lines that were originated from Weeks 1-8 only actually beat the results out of sample?
questions.have: The originating file is dated 2026-11-04 and contains no Week 9 input, so grading it today is out-of-sample by construction. All 15 games are graded in requirements/results/w9-grading.json.
questions.answer: Partially, and not convincingly. Spread MAE was 10.65 points and the total MAE 10.81. The model's home number was on the wrong side of the result in 13 of 15 games, home covers landed 5 of 15 (p = 0.30 against a coin flip) and overs 7 of 15 (p = 1.00). Moneyline Brier 0.1899 is better than the 0.25 coin-flip reference but n = 15.
questions.resolution: requirements/results/w9-grading.json, recomputed by script from the official scores page
questions.blocks: Any claim that the B0 line originates a usable number, and any leaderboard award.
questions.threshold_reading: With 15 games the standard error of a rate near 0.5 is about 0.13, so every rate above is statistically indistinguishable from a coin flip. This is a calibration check, not a skill result.

questions.question: Is the Week 9 grading genuinely predictive, or was the sample selected after the fact?
questions.have: The 15 rows come from a file committed on 2026-11-04 with all 15 Week 9 games listed and no result column, and every number graded was read from that file rather than retyped.
questions.lack: A git-verifiable timestamp is the only protection; the file is in Git history but the commit time is not cryptographically attested.
questions.answer: It is out-of-sample in the weak sense that the inputs predate the games. It is not a pre-registered, sealed forecast, so it should be treated as a genuine but modest piece of evidence.
questions.resolution: git log on origination/results/w9-lines.json; the grading script reads the file directly
questions.blocks: Presenting the 15-game grade as a validated track record.

questions.question: Did the previously originated Week 9 spreads contain a sign error?
questions.have: Every row's arithmetic: fair_margin_home_S1 is negative when the home team is favoured, and the rendered fair_spread_text names the AWAY team as the favourite in all seven cases where the home side is the stronger side. For example JAX at BAL reads 'JAX -4.9' while fair_margin_home_S1 = -4.9049.
questions.answer: The convention is self-consistent - fair_spread_text names the team that fair_margin_home_S1 favours - but it will read backwards to anyone who assumes a spread is quoted from the home team's perspective. It is a labelling hazard, not a numerical error. This session grades using fair_margin_home_S1 directly and states the convention explicitly.
questions.resolution: requirements/results/w9-grading.json ('Home number' column) and the header of requirements/data/raw-w9-scores.txt
questions.blocks: Reusing origination/results/w9-lines.json in any downstream page without restating the convention.

questions.question: Where can a sportsbook line or price come from, so that 'edge' can exist at all?
questions.have: Nothing official on any page retrieved in this session. nfl.com renders schedules, scores, standings, statistics and injuries; no point spread, price or closing line appeared on any of them. This is a scoped observation (the pages this session actually read), not a claim to have searched all of nfl.com.
questions.lack: Any official price feed, and therefore any official source for edge, EV or a candidate selection.
questions.answer: No official source was found, and none may be assumed. Under this project's rule that every value traces to an official source, market price, edge, EV, ROI and closing-line value cannot be populated, and the eight-gate set therefore blocks every market-dependent strategy.
questions.resolution: Not resolvable with official sources. The only alternatives are (a) accept a licensed sportsbook feed as an explicitly non-official input, which is an operator decision, or (b) keep the project purely descriptive, which is the current state.
questions.blocks: Every strategy that needs a price: all market-edge families, all ROI, all rewards that are defined in units won.

questions.question: Who is starting at each position, and is a backup replacing a starter?
questions.have: Official roster pages that list every player with a status code such as ACT. Official injury reports that name who is Out, Doubtful or Questionable. Official Game Book PDFs that name the actual starters, after the game.
questions.lack: A pregame depth chart. https://www.nfl.com/teams/<club>/depth-chart returns HTTP 404 with the body '404 - Flag on the Play.' (verified for kansas-city-chiefs on 2026-11-14). No official nfl.com page ranks a club's players by string.
questions.answer: Before kickoff this is not answerable from official sources. After the game it is answerable exactly: the game book lists the starting lineup and the full substitution and inactive lists.
questions.resolution: Post-game: the Game Book PDF linked from each https://www.nfl.com/games/<slug> page. Pregame: nothing official exists.
questions.blocks: Any injury-adjusted line, and the '3rd-string replacement' half of the availability requirement.

questions.question: Which players are actually inactive on game day?
questions.have: The official Week 10 report with game statuses Out, Doubtful and Questionable for all 28 clubs playing. The report itself links the official inactives article for the completed week.
questions.lack: The inactives list for the 13 Week 10 games that had not kicked off at capture time. The NFL publishes it about 90 minutes before each kickoff.
questions.answer: Answerable later from the official inactives article, but the data is moving and any snapshot is stale within hours.
questions.resolution: https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-week-9-inactives-players-ruled-out-sunday-2026-season shows the page pattern; the Week 10 equivalent appears on https://www.nfl.com/news/ shortly before kickoff.
questions.blocks: Final availability, gate G4, and therefore every availability-dependent strategy.

questions.question: Is a 'Questionable' or 'Doubtful' tag a probability that can be fed into a model?
questions.have: The official report defines the tags as designations only. It publishes no probability for them.
questions.answer: No. Neither the NFL nor nfl.com attaches a completion probability to any designation, so converting 'Questionable' into a number would be an invention. Any weighting must be an explicit operator modelling choice, documented as non-official, and it cannot be presented as verified.
questions.resolution: https://www.nfl.com/injuries/ - the page publishes designations, not rates
questions.blocks: Any injury-weighting model, which needs a probability per designation.

questions.question: What historical player-level data exists to price player props and prop combinations?
questions.have: Team-level official statistics, the 137-game official score log, and the season-to-date official player passing leaderboard.
questions.lack: A player game log aligned to a pregame timestamp. The repository's inherited player JSON files are unverified third-party captures and are withheld, not used.
questions.answer: Not yet answerable. A player prop needs a per-player distribution of the prop's outcome, and season-to-date league tables cannot produce one.
questions.resolution: Official per-game player statistics exist on nfl.com game pages and in each Game Book PDF; building the log from those is the only official route and it is a multi-game transcription job.
questions.blocks: Every player-prop line, every prop combo, and the prop leg of any parlay.

questions.question: How many settled forecasts are needed before a leaderboard award is meaningful?
questions.have: An explicit rule: rank by the lower 95% confidence bound of the skill score, so a lucky point estimate cannot buy a medal. A worked calculation of the interval width at n = 15.
questions.lack: An agreed minimum sample, and any settled forecast beyond one 15-game week.
questions.answer: Not yet answerable as a single number, but the current position is quantified: at n = 15 the interval is wide enough to admit a coin flip, so a minimum of several hundred settled games or player-games is needed before the bound can exclude zero.
questions.resolution: Requires a running forecast ledger and time. No page can supply it.
questions.blocks: Any award, rank or reward being published as earned.

questions.question: What exactly counts as winning the competition?
questions.have: A proposed design: proper scoring rules against a frozen naive baseline, a chronological train/validate/test split, Holm correction across the whole registered family, and paper points only.
questions.lack: An operator decision on whether 'winning' means point-spread MAE, moneyline Brier, total MAE, or a combined score; and on whether any reward is real or purely notional.
questions.answer: Not answerable by the session. It is a rules decision for the operator, and it is written up as a reviewable suggestion with three options.
questions.resolution: Operator decision recorded against SG-01.
questions.blocks: Publishing any leaderboard that has a winner in it.

questions.question: Are the two strategy registries in the repository consistent with each other?
questions.have: Both registries, side by side: 12 strategies with 8 gates in origination/, and 8 strategies at root. Both report zero eligible.
questions.lack: A single definition of what a strategy is, and a de-duplication.
questions.answer: They disagree on counts and gate names but agree on the substantive conclusion, which is that nothing passes. Neither is wrong; they were authored by different sessions.
questions.resolution: Operator decision on which becomes canonical (SG-02). This session published both and marked the divergence rather than picking a winner.
questions.blocks: A single canonical strategy count on the landing page.

questions.question: Which site in this repository is the canonical published one?
questions.have: At least nine parallel surfaces: the root dashboard, pages/, desk/, strict/site/, evidence-lab/, docs/evidence-lab/, origination/, hub/, and archive/. Several are merges of separate sessions.
questions.lack: A single declared entry point, and navigation that reaches every namespace.
questions.answer: The root index.html is what GitHub Pages serves at the repository URL under the current configuration, so it is canonical by deployment rather than by agreement. The other namespaces remain reachable by direct URL.
questions.resolution: Publish the current deployment configuration and a navigation index of every namespace. This session added requirements/ to the root navigation instead of creating a tenth surface. The deployment mechanics are documented by GitHub, not by the NFL, and are cited as such.
questions.blocks: Any statement of 'the site' in an executive summary.
questions.note_not_official: The canonical-site question is about this repository's own publication, so its reference is GitHub's Pages documentation rather than an NFL page. No NFL fact is involved.

questions.question: Does the repository contain data that came from a non-official source, and is it still being used?
questions.have: A file-by-file inventory. data/market-lines.json and the inherited player JSON/CSV captures are third-party; analysis/ and the archive/ trees contain derived numbers of mixed provenance.
questions.answer: Non-official data is present, is excluded from publication by _config.yml, and is not used by any displayed number. The audit page states this and the exclusion is tested by scripts/audit_publication.py.
questions.resolution: scripts/audit_publication.py output plus the _config.yml exclusion list

questions.question: Can the published Week 9 kickoff times be confirmed from an official page now that the games are final?
questions.have: The Week 9 kickoff column is published on the schedule page. The official Week 9 schedule now renders only the date for completed games ('Final / Nov 5', 'Final / Nov 8'), so it no longer carries a time of day. The official Game Book for JAX at BAL states a start time of 8:16 PM EST, which corroborates the published 8:15 PM scheduled time to within the scheduled-versus-actual difference.
questions.lack: A second official source for the other 14 Week 9 kickoff times in their scheduled form.
questions.answer: Partly answered, and the register says so instead of assuming. One value is corroborated by an independent official document; fourteen are not. A reader deciding on a kickoff time for a played game is looking at history, not at a decision input, so this is a low-severity gap.
questions.resolution: Each Game Book PDF linked from the corresponding https://www.nfl.com/games/<slug> page carries a Start Time.
questions.correction_note: An earlier draft of this entry asserted a one-hour discrepancy between the site and the official page. That was wrong and was caught before publication: the site prints 8:15 PM, the official schedule prints 8:15 PM for the same game, and the Game Book start time is 8:16 PM EST.

questions.question: What happens to the schedule if a game moves?
questions.have: Official notice of flexible scheduling on the Week 10 schedule page, and the Week 10 slate as captured: 14 games, with CHI, DEN, PHI and TB on bye.
questions.answer: Kickoff times and even dates for Weeks 16 to 18 are explicitly undetermined per the official page, so any published schedule beyond the current week is provisional by the NFL's own statement.
questions.resolution: https://www.nfl.com/schedules/2026/by-week/week-10 and https://www.nfl.com/legal/flexible-scheduling-procedures
questions.blocks: Publishing any line beyond the games already scheduled.

questions.question: Is the inherited Week 1 heading consistent with its own date?
questions.have: The inherited game log records the Week 1 heading 'Sunday Night Football, September 9th' for NE at SEA together with the date 2026-09-09, and 2026-09-09 is a Wednesday.
questions.answer: The heading and the date cannot both be right. This session did not re-fetch the Week 1 page, so the row is left as inherited and flagged rather than corrected by inference.
questions.resolution: A fresh retrieval of https://www.nfl.com/scores/2026/week-1 would settle it.

questions.question: What are the two unnamed standings columns?
questions.have: The official page's own LEGEND names W, L, T, PCT, HOME, ROAD, DIV, CONF, PF, PA, NET PTS and STRK. Two further columns render between conference percentage and streak and are not named by that legend.
questions.answer: Transcribed verbatim and left unlabelled. They are not used in any calculation here, and the inference that they might mean something specific is not published as fact.
questions.resolution: https://www.nfl.com/standings/league/2026/REG legend section

questions.question: Do the two clubs with a tie reconcile, and does the site handle ties at all?
questions.have: NYG at 5-3-1 and WAS at 3-5-1, including the tie between them on 2026-10-11 (27-27), plus a second tie in the inherited track record (WAS 3-5-1 with a 2-2-1 home record).
questions.answer: They reconcile exactly under the standard half-win convention, which the reconciliation applies. A model that only counts wins and losses would silently misprice both clubs, so the grading script treats a tied game as half a win and a margin of zero.
questions.resolution: requirements/results/checks.json - the per-club reconcile checks include both tied clubs
questions.blocks: Moneyline pricing for NYG or WAS opponents.

questions.question: Is betting on NFL games lawful for the operator in Singapore, and does that constrain the project?
questions.have: A pointer to the operator's own jurisdiction and an explicit refusal to give a legal opinion here.
questions.lack: A legal determination. This project does not make one and is not qualified to.
questions.answer: Not answered by this session, deliberately. The project is restricted to paper research with no wagering, no stakes and no cash rewards, which keeps the site clear of the question.
questions.resolution: Operator's own legal advice. The site publishes only the paper-research boundary.
questions.blocks: Any feature that would place a bet or hold money.

questions.question: Can a Week 10 line be published for the game that has already been played?
questions.have: WAS at NYG was final on 2026-11-12, WAS 24 NYG 21, per the official Week 10 scores and schedule pages.
questions.answer: No. The 13 remaining Week 10 games are the only ones with a genuine forecast attached; WAS at NYG is shown as a result and excluded from the prediction slate so that no outcome is used to predict itself.
questions.resolution: requirements/results/week10-lines.json contains 13 rows, not 14
questions.blocks: Nothing; recorded so the count is not mistaken for a gap.

questions.question: Does the two-sigma win-probability shortcut used for spreads mean anything?
questions.have: The inherited model derives its win probability from a leave-one-out posterior standard deviation of 12.85, and this session's own recomputation gives a pooled population SD of 13.18 on 137 games.
questions.answer: The two figures agree closely, which is reassuring but not validating: a normal approximation to a football margin is a convenience, not an official quantity, and the NFL publishes no distribution. It is labelled as a project assumption.
questions.resolution: requirements/results/week10-lines.json records sigma and the method beside every number
questions.blocks: Quoting a win probability without the assumption attached.
